menu.title: STORM ALERT
menu.subtitle: Crisis Management Simulation
menu.tagline: Every decision counts. Time is running out.
menu.aboutP1: A severe winter storm is closing in. Storm Alert is a preparedness simulation that puts you in the middle of a real crisis — at home, facing the disaster firsthand.
menu.aboutP2: Gather supplies, make decisions under pressure, and figure out who to call when things go wrong. Your choices determine how you and your household make it through the next 72 hours.

familySetup.heading: Who's in your household?
familySetup.subtitle: This shapes your preparation plan and the crisis you'll face.

112.title: Emergency Line
112.message:
"112, what is your emergency?"

You explain grandmother's condition.

"Sir, this line is for life-threatening emergencies. Your grandmother's situation, while concerning, is not immediately life-threatening. You're tying up resources needed for critical cases."

They transfer you, but it takes extra time. Help will arrive, but delayed.

1220.title: Family Doctor Advice Line
1220.message:
"Health advice line, how can I help?"

You explain grandmother's condition - weak, dehydrated, needs medical attention but stable.

"You did the right thing calling. Based on what you're describing, she needs fluids and monitoring. I'm connecting you with crisis medical support who can send someone to check on her."

Within the hour, a medical team arrives. They stabilize grandmother and praise your quick thinking.

You called the right number for the right situation.

1247.title: Rescue Coordination
1247.message:
"Rescue coordination, how can we help?"

You explain grandmother's condition.

"We can dispatch assistance, but for medical advice you should call 1220 - the family doctor line. They can better assess her condition. We'll still send someone, but it may take longer as we're prioritizing rescue operations."

Help arrives, but a direct call to 1220 would have been faster and more appropriate.

1343.title: Power Outage Line
1343.message:
"Power outage reporting line. Please hold..."

[Automated menu plays]

"Press 1 to report an outage. Press 2 to check restoration status..."

This isn't what you need. You hang up and lose precious time.

What was the health advice number again?

default.title: Number Not Recognized
default.message:
Beep... beep... beep...

"The number you have dialed is not in service."

That number doesn't exist. You need one of the real emergency lines.

1220.title: Family Doctor Advice Line
1220.message:
"Health advice line, how can I help?"

You explain the situation — your relative is weak, dizzy, blood pressure feels wrong. Not life-threatening, but they need help and the roads are blocked.

"You did the right thing calling. Based on what you're describing, they need fluids and monitoring. I'm connecting you with crisis medical support who can send someone directly to you."

Within the hour, a medical team arrives. They stabilize your relative and check on you both.

You called the right number for the right situation.

1247.title: Rescue Coordination
1247.message:
"Rescue coordination, how can we help?"

You explain the situation — your relative is in distress, the children need you there, the roads are blocked. You need someone to come to you.

"Understood. We handle exactly this — coordinating rescue when people can't leave. We're dispatching a team to your address now."

A rescue team arrives within the hour. They help stabilize your relative on site and confirm your address is safe.

You called the right number.

112.title: Emergency Line
112.message:
"112, what is your emergency?"

You explain the situation.

"We can try to help. For coordinating a rescue team to come to you, 1247 is actually the right number — but we'll pass this along."

It takes longer than it should. Help eventually arrives, but the coordination wasn't ideal.

1220.title: Family Doctor Advice Line
1220.message:
"Health advice line, how can I help?"

You explain the situation — your relative is in serious distress, you can't leave because of the children, you need someone to come.

"I can give medical advice, but coordinating a physical rescue is outside what we do. You need to call 1247 — rescue coordination. They can send a team directly to you."

You lose precious time. What was the rescue number again?

1343.title: Power Outage Line
1343.message:
"Power outage reporting line. Please hold..."

[Automated menu plays]

"Press 1 to report an outage. Press 2 to check restoration status..."

This isn't what you need at all. You hang up, frustrated.

What was the rescue coordination number again?

default.title: Number Not Recognized
default.message:
Beep... beep... beep...

"The number you have dialed is not in service."

That number doesn't exist. You need the line that sends help directly to you.

112.title: Emergency Services
112.message:
"112, what is your emergency?"

You describe the situation — your child has broken out in hives, throat is swelling, can't breathe properly.

"This is anaphylaxis. Keep them calm and upright. Do you have an EpiPen? An ambulance is on the way — keep this line open."

The paramedics arrive and administer epinephrine immediately. Your child stabilizes.

112 was exactly the right call for a life-threatening emergency.

1220.title: Family Doctor Advice Line
1220.message:
"Health advice line, how can I help?"

You describe the swelling throat, the hives.

"This sounds like anaphylaxis — this is a life-threatening emergency. You need to call 112 immediately. Every second counts. Hang up and call 112 now."

You lose precious seconds. What was the emergency number again?

1247.title: Rescue Coordination
1247.message:
"Rescue coordination, how can we help?"

You describe your child's condition.

"This is a medical emergency — you need 112 immediately. We coordinate logistics, not medical emergencies. Call 112 now."

You lose precious time. What was the emergency number again?

1343.title: Power Outage Line
1343.message:
"Power outage reporting line. Please hold..."

[Automated menu plays]

You hang up immediately. Wrong number entirely.

Your child needs emergency help. What was that number?

default.title: Number Not Recognized
default.message:
Beep... beep... beep...

"The number you have dialed is not in service."

Your child needs help right now. That number doesn't exist — try the right emergency line.

1343.title: Power Outage Reporting
1343.message:
"Power outage reporting. What's your address?"

You report the outage and mention you've been without power for over 12 hours. You're starting to feel the cold — lightheaded and numb.

"Thank you. We're logging this area as a priority — there's been widespread outage. We also have a welfare check team. I'm noting your address."

Within hours, a welfare check arrives. The power comes back on by evening.

1343 was exactly the right number.

112.title: Emergency Line
112.message:
"112, what is your emergency?"

You explain you've had no power for 12 hours, feeling lightheaded and cold.

"For power outages, please call 1343 — that's the dedicated line. If your condition worsens to a medical emergency, call back here. For now, keep warm and call 1343."

They log the call but it adds to their load. You need to try 1343.

1220.title: Family Doctor Advice Line
1220.message:
"Health advice line, how can I help?"

You explain the situation — power out, feeling lightheaded.

"For power outages, you need to call 1343. If you're feeling faint, that could be from cold — keep warm, drink water. But the outage itself should be reported to 1343."

Not the right number for this. Try 1343.

1247.title: Rescue Coordination
1247.message:
"Rescue coordination, how can we help?"

You explain the situation.

"For power outages, please call 1343 — the power company's emergency line. If you need physical rescue, call back. For now, contact 1343."

Not the right number. Try 1343.

default.title: Number Not Recognized
default.message:

"The number you have dialed is not in service."

That number doesn't exist. Try one of the real emergency lines.

sms.body: A severe storm warning has been issued for your region. Significant power outages, disrupted water supply, and road closures are anticipated in the coming hours.
sms.body2: Secure adequate supplies of drinking water, non-perishable food, medications, emergency lighting, and a heat source. Stay indoors and monitor official broadcast channels for further instructions.

radioBroadcast.title: Emergency Broadcast
radioBroadcast.line1: This is an emergency broadcast from the National Crisis Center.
radioBroadcast.line2: A severe storm is affecting coastal regions. Power outages have been reported across multiple districts.
radioBroadcast.line3: Stay indoors. Conserve phone battery. Check on elderly neighbors if safe to do so.
radioBroadcast.hint: 🗒️ Write these numbers down — you may need them later.

store.warningBody: The storm is closing in. You don't have time to browse — grab only what you genuinely need and get out.
store.warningRule: The trip to the store and back costs 20 minutes. Each item you pick up costs 1 more. Choose wisely.
store.headerSubtitle: Grab what you need before the storm hits

essentials.label: Essentials
essentials.description: Some are must-haves — others depend on what you already have

food.label: Food & Drink
food.description: Choose non-perishables that don't need refrigeration

matches.name: Waterproof Matches
matches.feedback: Handy backup, but a lighter does the same job for less. Worth having if you have no lighter.

power_bank.name: Power Bank
power_bank.feedback: Gives your phone a few extra charges, but AA batteries last far longer for radios and torches.

hand_sanitizer.name: Hand Sanitizer
hand_sanitizer.feedback: Useful when the tap is dry, but stored water and soap does the same job and costs less.

radio_manual.name: Hand-crank Radio
radio_manual.feedback: Works without batteries — a genuine backup. But if you already have AA batteries, a standard battery radio is lighter and easier.

whistle.name: Emergency Whistle
whistle.feedback: Vital if you might need outdoor rescue, but low priority if you're sheltering at home.

scented_candle.name: Scented Candle
scented_candle.feedback: It gives some light, but melts faster than proper emergency candles and won't last the night.

dried.name: Dried Foods
dried.feedback: Pasta and rice need cooking — oats are fine as-is.

instant_noodles.name: Instant Noodles
instant_noodles.feedback: You'll need a heat source and water to prepare these.

frozen.name: Frozen Meals
frozen.feedback: No power = no freezer. These will spoil within hours.

milk.name: Fresh Milk
milk.feedback: Spoils fast without a fridge. Buy UHT milk instead.

fresh.name: Fresh Vegetables
fresh.feedback: Will wilt and rot without refrigeration.

yogurt.name: Yogurt
yogurt.feedback: Needs to stay cold — it won't last.

sushi.name: Fresh Sushi
sushi.feedback: Raw fish spoils dangerously fast without refrigeration.

birthday_cake.name: Birthday Cake
birthday_cake.feedback: Perishable, heavy, and not exactly survival food.

board_game.name: Board Game
board_game.feedback: Fair enough — at least it doesn't need electricity.

book.name: Paperback Book
book.feedback: Not a bad choice — books work in the dark with a candle.

cigarettes.name: Cigarettes
cigarettes.feedback: A fire hazard and health risk — the last thing you need right now.

alcohol.name: Beer & Wine
alcohol.feedback: Alcohol impairs judgment exactly when you need it most. And it dehydrates you.

energy_drink.name: Energy Drinks
energy_drink.feedback: Loaded with sugar and caffeine — will spike and crash your energy.

video_games.name: Video Games
video_games.feedback: No power, no gaming. This stays on the shelf.

tv.name: New Television
tv.feedback: You can't carry this, and there's no power anyway.

fashion.name: Fashion Clothes
fashion.feedback: Style won't keep you warm when the heating dies.

perfume.name: Luxury Perfume
perfume.feedback: Smelling great won't help you survive the storm.

espresso.name: Espresso Machine
espresso.feedback: Needs electricity and running water. Leave it.

flowers.name: Fresh Flowers
flowers.feedback: These will wilt before the storm even hits.

sunglasses.name: Designer Sunglasses
sunglasses.feedback: Hard to see the appeal when there's a storm coming.

gym_weights.name: Dumbbells
gym_weights.feedback: Great in normal life — completely useless right now.

homeSetup.subtitle: Tell us about where you live — it shapes how the cold hits

homeSetup.summarySubtitle: What matters most for keeping warm
homeSetup.weakSpotsTitle: Weak spots to seal before the storm
homeSetup.weakSpotsEmpty: No obvious weak spots — still seal up before the storm.

fixedLabels.detached: A detached house loses heat on every side — seal hard and pick one room to hold warmth.
fixedLabels.rural: An older or rural house tends to leak heat — sealing and a backup heat source matter more here.
fixedLabels.exposed_layout: A top-floor, corner, or freestanding home is more exposed to the cold — you can't change that, so plan to compensate: seal thoroughly and concentrate heat in one room.

tipLabels.no_stove_aspirational: No wood stove or gas? Sealing and a warm room cover ~80% of the win. A stove is gold if you ever add one.
tipLabels.apartment_neighbors: In a flat, your neighbors' walls help — close doors to less-used rooms to use that warmth.

heatNote.title: Your home priorities
heatNote.writeDown: Write these priorities in your notebook — you'll want them when the storm hits.

tips.no_stove: No wood stove or gas means you can't make new heat once the power's out — so keep the heat you have: seal the house and set up one warm room (the actions below).

gapLabels.no_flashlight: No dedicated flashlight (the #1 thing to own)

gapLabels.candles_no_matches: Candles but no matches or lighter — keep a way to light them with them

tipLabels.candle_safety: Candles are backup only — open flame is a top cause of outage fires. Never leave one unattended.
tipLabels.battery_rotation: Keep spare batteries in the sizes your devices use, and rotate old stock so it's never flat.

tips.candle_safety: Using candles? Keep them away from anything that burns and never leave them unattended.

rumorSort.title: Signal vs Noise
rumorSort.subtitle: Messages are flooding in as the storm builds. What do you do with each?
rumorSort.takeaway: Trust official sources — an EE-ALARM phone alert, the emergency broadcast on Vikerraadio, or kriis.ee. Verify anything plausible but unconfirmed before acting on it. Ignore — and never forward — messages built on urgency, secrecy, or 'share now'. In a crisis, a rumour you spread can do real harm.

gov_alert.text: Government emergency alert: severe storm overnight. Stay indoors. Power outages of 24–48h possible. Follow official channels.
gov_alert.why: This is the official public warning system. Trust it and act on it.

water_poison.text: 🚨 The tap water is CONTAMINATED across the city!! Authorities are hiding it — SHARE before this gets deleted!!
water_poison.why: Urgency, secrecy, 'share before it's deleted', and no official source — a textbook rumour. Don't act on it, and don't spread it.

free_fuel.text: My neighbour says the petrol station on the corner is giving out free fuel — huge queue already.
free_fuel.why: Plausible, but it's hearsay that could send a dangerous crowd rushing out. Don't pass it on; check an official source before acting.

radio_advice.text: Emergency broadcast: the Rescue Board advises charging your devices now and checking on elderly neighbours. Power is expected back within ~36 hours.
radio_advice.why: The official emergency broadcaster carrying authorities' advice. Trustworthy — act on it.

chain_forward.text: ⚠ Forward this to 10 people within the hour or the emergency alert network will shut down in your area!
chain_forward.why: A chain-letter scare. Real alert systems don't work this way. Ignore it and never forward it.

bridge_photo.text: A photo is going around of a collapsed bridge on the main road — is it real?
bridge_photo.why: A photo can be old or from somewhere else entirely. Verify against official info before believing or sharing it.

cabinetCheck.title: Sort This Medicine Shelf
cabinetCheck.subtitle: Practise here first — read each label and judge it against the next 6 months, not just this storm.
cabinetCheck.hint: Tap an item to read its label.

verdictHints.keep: Good and enough — nothing to buy
verdictHints.restock: Fine, but running low — buy more, keep this
verdictHints.toss: Expired or unsafe — throw out AND buy new

cabinetCheck.takeaway: Check expiry dates twice a year. Keep a 7-day buffer of any prescription. Bin expired medicines — return old antibiotics and adrenaline pens to a pharmacy, never the bin. And know which medicines must stay cold if the power fails.

painkillers.name: Painkillers
painkillers.why: That date was 8 months ago. Expired painkillers lose strength — bin them and add a fresh box to your list.

plasters.name: Plasters
plasters.why: Years left on the date and plenty in the box. Keep it — the backbone of your first-aid kit.

antiseptic.name: Antiseptic
antiseptic.why: The date is fine — the bottle isn't. Nearly out, so restock it. You'll want it for cleaning cuts when you can't just pop to a clinic.

allergy.name: Allergy tablets
allergy.why: That date passed last month. Bin it — and if anyone reacts to pollen, dust or stings, replace it so it works when needed.

vitamins.name: Daily vitamins
vitamins.why: Nine months left and plenty in the jar — fine to keep. Just don't let it crowd out the medicines that actually matter in a crisis.

bp_pills.name: Blood-pressure pills
bp_pills.why: The date is nearly a year off, but that's not the problem — this is a daily prescription with 5 tablets left. Restock now and keep a 7-day buffer, so a closed pharmacy never catches you out.

insulin.name: Insulin
insulin.why: Date and quantity are both fine — keep it. The catch is cold: in an outage the fridge holds about 4 hours closed, then move it to a cool bag with ice packs. Ask your pharmacist how long yours can be out.

fever_syrup.name: Child's fever syrup
fever_syrup.why: That date is next month — it won't see out the winter. Replace it now so it's ready if a fever hits mid-storm.

epipen.name: Adrenaline pen (EpiPen)
epipen.why: That date passed 2 months ago, and an expired adrenaline pen may not work in a severe allergic reaction. Replace it straight away and keep it where everyone can find it — this is a 112 situation.

crisisScreen.nightSubtitle: The power is out. The storm has taken down the lines.
crisisScreen.morningSubtitle: The taps are dead. The fridge is warming. The stove won't turn on.
crisisScreen.pipeWarning: ⚠️ You hear a creak from the pipes — they could freeze and burst.
crisisScreen.pipeTip: A slow drip helps: moving water freezes slower.

good.headline: Help is on the way.
elderlyAndChildren: Within the hour, a rescue team arrives.
They stabilize {{elderlyName}} on site and check on the children.
"You did the right thing — calling 1247 brought a team directly to you."
You were prepared. You paid attention. And when it mattered, you knew exactly what to do.
elderly: Within the hour, a medical team arrives.
They check on {{elderlyName}} thoroughly. "Dehydrated but stable."
"You did exactly the right thing calling the health advice line."
You were prepared. You paid attention. And when it mattered, you knew exactly what to do.
children: "You called the right number. A few more minutes and this could have been much worse."
Your child stabilizes. You breathe again.
solo: The power company logs your report as a priority area.
By afternoon, a welfare check team arrives.
"Good call using 1343 — that's exactly what it's for."
The power comes back on by evening.

water.label: Water
water.description: The taps are still running — but if the power goes out, the electric pump stops. Fill containers now before you lose access.

food.label: Food
food.description: The fridge will stop working when the power cuts. Stock up on canned goods and dry food that doesn't need cooking or refrigeration.

heat.label: Heat
heat.description: Central heating runs on electricity. If the grid fails, temperatures will drop fast — especially at night. Have a backup heat source ready.

light.label: Light
light.description: When the lights go out, your phone becomes your only torch — and it drains fast. A flashlight with spare batteries keeps you safe without burning your battery.

info.label: Info
info.description: The internet and mobile networks may go down. A battery-powered radio is the only reliable way to receive emergency broadcasts and official updates.

medication.label: Meds
medication.description: Pharmacies may close and roads may be impassable. If anyone in your household depends on regular medication, make sure you have enough to last the storm.

shop.label: Shop
shop.description: Buy water, food, and batteries at the grocery store.

done.label: Done
done.description: Stop preparing and face the oncoming storm.
